Corporate Governance Dilemmas

The Letter
and the Spirit.

Legal vs. Ethical
Letter of the Law vs. Spirit of the Law

A case study of OpenAI, 2015–2023.
One mission. One unusual board.
Five days that tested both.

FRIDAY · 17 NOVEMBER 2023 · 12:00 PM

Imagine you run the most talked-about company on earth. You get a text asking you to join a video call. The whole board is there, except your co-founder. Within minutes, you are fired. The reason, in the board's own words:

"not consistently candid"

No details for the staff. Minutes of notice for Microsoft, the biggest investor. And the board had every legal right to do it. So how does a company end up here?

RewindTo answer that, we go back to 2015, and to a promise.

December 2015 · The promise

OpenAI's mission:

Ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity.

"…the way that is most likely to benefit humanity as a whole, unconstrained by a need to generate financial return."OpenAI founding statement, 2015
Key term

Artificial general intelligence (AGI): an AI system that can match or outperform humans at most economically valuable work.

The promise

A nonprofit. Build value "for everyone rather than shareholders." Publish the research. Share the patents.

Why people joined

"I turned down offers for multiple times the dollar amount I accepted."
Ilya Sutskever, co-founder

2019 · The mission meets the bill

Changing the world turned out to be very expensive.

$1bn

Pledged in 2015. Not enough to pay for the computing power and talent that AI research needs.

100×

The cap on investor returns in the new "capped-profit" company. Anything above the cap goes to the nonprofit.

~$13bn

Invested by Microsoft from 2019 to 2023, for a minority economic interest and no board seat.

"Donations alone would not scale with the cost of computational power and talent required to push core research forward, jeopardizing our mission."OpenAI, 2019
Mission linkOpenAI took the money to protect the mission. Now profit and mission lived under one roof.
The theory · Bob Tricker

So who is in charge? The board.

"If management is about running the business, governance is about seeing that it is run properly."Bob Tricker

In Tricker's model, the board sits between the owners and the managers. Owners provide capital and elect the board. The board directs and supervises management. The board answers to the owners.

Framework: Tricker, B. (2010). Corporate Governance: Principles, Policies, and Practices.
OpenAI's structure

Tricker's model, turned upside down.

Normally, owners elect the board, and the board answers to them.

At OpenAI, a nonprofit board sat above the owners. Its directors held no equity. It answered to the mission.

Pre-read · Mayer (2021)Foundations already own companies to protect a founder's purpose: Bosch, Carlsberg, IKEA, Tata. OpenAI's design had precedent.
Mission linkThe structure put the mission in charge. The open question: who speaks for the mission?
Source: HKU Case HK1445, Exhibit 1 (from OpenAI, "OpenAI LP"). Layers mapped to Tricker (2010).
Back to 17 November 2023

Six seats. Four votes.

Three insiders, all co-founders. Three independent directors, two of them linked to effective altruism, a movement that puts AI safety first.

Independent director: a board member with no management role or ownership ties to the company.

The deciding vote came from an insider. Co-founder Ilya Sutskever sided with the three independents.

17–21 November 2023

A script Hollywood would die to write.

0/770

employees signed one letter: resign, or we leave.

Fri 17

Fired.

Altman removed by a simple majority. Brockman quits. CTO Mira Murati named interim CEO.

Sat 18

Exodus.

Senior researchers resign. Altman's camp sets a 5 p.m. deadline. The board misses it.

Sun 19

Plot twist.

Emmett Shear, ex-CEO of Twitch, becomes CEO number three. Near midnight, Microsoft hires Altman.

Mon 20

Revolt.

The staff letter lands. Sutskever, who led the firing: "I deeply regret my participation."

Tue 21

Return.

Altman is back. The old board is gone, except D'Angelo. Bret Taylor (ex-Salesforce co-CEO) and Larry Summers (ex-US Treasury Secretary) join.

Mission linkThe people who joined for the mission sided with the CEO, not with the board that guarded it.
21 November 2023 · The new board

Three seats. A very different kind of board.

New · Chair

Bret Taylor

Former co-CEO of Salesforce. Former CTO of Facebook. Chaired Twitter's board when Musk bought it.

New

Larry Summers

Economist. Former US Treasury Secretary under Clinton. Former president of Harvard.

Stayed · the only survivor

Adam D'Angelo

CEO of Quora. The one director who voted to fire Altman and kept his seat.

Before: three co-founders and three safety-minded independents.
After: experienced corporate and policy figures.

Gone: Toner, McCauley and Sutskever. Brockman returned as president, not director. Altman returned as CEO and rejoined the board in March 2024.

Mission linkThe new board looked like a normal company's board. Was that a fix, or a retreat from the mission?
The yardstick

Three principles. Three questions for the board.

Corporate governance is the system of rules and processes used to direct and oversee a company. We judge the board against three of its core principles.

Principle 01

Fairness

Treat shareholders, employees, partners and communities with equal consideration.

Were all stakeholders treated with equal consideration?

Principle 02

Transparency

Give timely, accurate and clear information on performance, conflicts and risks.

Did the board share clear reasons, on time?

Principle 03

Accountability

Explain the purpose of the company's actions and the results of its conduct.

Did the board explain its decision, and answer for it?

NextThree dilemmas show where these principles came under strain.
Source: Investopedia, "Corporate Governance: Definition, Principles, Models, and Examples." Two further principles, responsibility and risk management, are not the focus here.
Dilemma 01 · Legal vs. Ethical

The law sets the floor.
Ethics sets the ceiling.

Legal asks: "Are we allowed?"
Ethical asks: "Should we?"

Most governance failures are not illegal. They sit in the grey zone: allowed, but not right.

Ethical
Unethical
Legal

Legal & ethical

The goal. Compliant and defensible.

Legal, but unethical?

Allowed on paper. Questioned by almost everyone affected.

OpenAI board, Nov 2023
Illegal

Illegal, but ethical

Whistleblowing, civil disobedience. Rare in boardrooms.

Illegal & unethical

Fraud. Enron is the classic example.

Mission linkThe board did not defend itself with the law. It defended itself with the mission.
Dilemma 02 · Letter of the Law vs. Spirit of the Law

The board followed the letter. Did it honour the spirit?

The letter

The charter gave the board full authority. A majority vote was enough. The mission outranked profit. On paper, every step was valid.

"The destruction of the company could be consistent with the board's mission."Helen Toner, board member

The spirit

Governance exists to protect stakeholders through transparency and accountability. The staff got no reasons. The biggest investor got minutes of notice.

"It cannot be your duty to allow the company to die."Jason Kwon, Chief Strategy Officer
Mission linkBoth sides quoted the same mission. They disagreed about what it demanded.
Dilemma 03 · Rules-based vs. Principles-based

Tick the box, or use your judgement?

Rules-basedPrinciples-based
Core ideaDetailed, prescriptive requirements. Bright lines.Broad outcomes. Directors decide how to meet them.
ExampleUS Sarbanes-Oxley Act (2002), passed after Enron's board waived conflict-of-interest safeguards.UK Corporate Governance Code: "comply or explain."
StrengthClear, measurable, easy to enforce.Flexible. Fits unusual structures and new situations.
WeaknessInvites loopholes: "it wasn't against the rules."Vague. Depends on the integrity of the people applying it.
OpenAIFew hard rules bound the board. None were broken.One principle, the mission, which each side read differently.
Pre-read · Mayer (2021)Rules struggle in fast technology. Regulators are "less well informed than the companies they are regulating," and technology leaves regulation "increasingly far behind."
Part IV · Class activity

The debate.

Two teams · One motion · Class vote

For: the letter of the rules. Against: the spirit of good governance.

The debate

The motion:

This house believes the OpenAI board was right to fire Sam Altman.

For · The letter
MandateThe charter made the board answer to the mission, not to investors. Directors held no equity for exactly this reason.
TrustA board cannot supervise a CEO it does not trust. The board said Altman was "not consistently candid."
SafetyThe nonprofit was built to say no to commercial pressure. That is what it did.
Against · The spirit
FairnessNo specific charge, no hearing, and minutes of notice for the CEO and the main investor.
TransparencyThe board never explained its decision. It lost 747 of 770 staff, and one of its own voters.
OutcomeIt nearly destroyed the organisation that carries the mission, and was reversed within five days.
FormatOpening, 2 minutes per side · Rebuttal, 1 minute per side · Class vote · Then, our answer.
What the pre-reads tell us

OpenAI had a purpose. It did not have a precise one.

Mayer (2021) · The economics of purpose
"Purpose should be neither mundane nor aspirational."
PrecisionA real purpose states which problems it solves, for whom, and how. "Benefit all of humanity" states none of these.
TrustTrust comes from clarity plus credible commitment. OpenAI had the commitment, but not the clarity.
AccountabilityWith a purpose, the board's accountability "extends to a wider body of beneficiaries," not only to owners.
Investopedia · The 4 Ps of governance

Purpose

Strong, but too broad to guide a decision.

People

Loyal to the CEO, not to the board.

Process

Missing: no rules for disclosure or succession.

Performance

World-leading: ChatGPT started the AI race.

The UK Corporate Governance Code, quoted by Mayer: the board should ensure that purpose, values, strategy and culture "are aligned." At OpenAI, 747 of 770 staff showed they were not.

Sources: Mayer, C. (2021). The Future of the Corporation and the Economics of Purpose. Journal of Management Studies, 58(3). Investopedia, "Corporate Governance." Grades are our own assessment.
The three principles · applied to the OpenAI board

The board fired its CEO for not being candid. Then it was not candid with anyone.

Fairness
Weak.

Altman got minutes of notice and no specific charge. The staff got no reasons. Microsoft, with about $13bn invested, got a phone call minutes before the announcement.

Transparency
Absent.

The board said Altman had not been candid, but said it could not elaborate "for legal reasons." No evidence was shared with staff, investors or the public.

Accountability
Forced from outside.

The board never answered for the decision through any process. The staff and Microsoft held it to account instead: within five days, most of the board was replaced.

Source: HKU Case HK1445. Grades are our own assessment, for discussion.

Strong on power. Weak on process.

Past & present
Future
Outward
Conformance

Accountability

Explain to owners and stakeholders what was done, and why.

Failed.

The board never explained its decision to staff, investors or the public.

Performance

Strategy

Set the long-term direction of the organisation.

Clear intent.

The board put the mission ahead of growth, as the charter required.

Inward
Conformance

Supervision

Monitor management. Hire, review and, if needed, remove the CEO.

Power, no plan.

The board used its power to remove the CEO, with no plan for the day after.

Performance

Policy

Set the policies and limits that management works within.

Missing.

No visible policy for decisions that conflict with the mission, a test the Investopedia pre-read names.

Framework: Tricker, B. (2010). Corporate Governance: Principles, Policies, and Practices. Grades are our own assessment, for discussion.
The answer

Right power. Wrong process. Unclear purpose.

Principles
Fairness
Weak.

Key stakeholders were not heard.

Transparency
Absent.

No specific reasons were given.

Accountability
Forced from outside.

Staff and investors replaced the board.

Dilemmas
Legal vs. Ethical
Legal. Contested.

Within the board's power. Unfair in its execution.

Letter vs. Spirit
Letter kept. Spirit broken.

The charter was followed. Its purpose was not served.

Rules vs. Principles
A principle, no rules.

"Benefit humanity" justified the act and defined nothing.

In the 4 Ps: strong on purpose, missing on process. The irony: the board built to protect the mission lost its seats within five days. Power without legitimacy does not last.

Back to the missionDid the board protect the mission, or only its right to decide?
Epilogue · after the case ends

Was it solved? Contained in 2023. Restructured in 2025.

Nov 2023 · The reversal
People changed.

Altman returned. Three of the four directors who fired him left. The structure, the broad mission and Microsoft's lack of a vote all stayed the same.

Mar 2024 · The review
Legal, not required.

An outside review by law firm WilmerHale found a breakdown of trust. The old board acted "within its broad discretion," but Altman's conduct "did not mandate removal." Altman rejoined the board, with three new directors.

Oct 2025 · The restructure
A new structure.

The company became a public benefit corporation. The nonprofit became the OpenAI Foundation, kept control and holds about 26%. Microsoft holds about 27%.

The communication failed in 2023. The structure is what changed afterwards. Did the mission survive, or did the letter win in the end?

Sources (after the case): OpenAI, "Review completed" (Mar 2024); Fortune (8 Mar 2024); OpenAI, "Statement on OpenAI's Nonprofit and PBC"; CNBC and Al Jazeera (28 Oct 2025).

Rules tell you what you can do.
Principles tell you what you should.

For discussion

1. Should a board act, even legally, if it cannot explain why?
2. Who does a mission-driven board answer to, if not owners?
3. Would rules have prevented this, or only better judgement?

OpenAI began with a promise to benefit all of humanity. It built an unusual structure to keep that promise. In November 2023, that structure was tested, and the letter and the spirit pulled apart.

So, what's your take?
